My estimate is commonly used short hand and is all inclusive, Walmart's initial success has a lot to do with successfully lowering the all inclusive labor costs to under 20% (if I recal 15% average, but that's an old factoid). That would increase my estimate to a whopping 36% labor contribution to total costs, far from torpedoing my point when extrapolated across the idea.
So you're saying that labor costs have a lot to do with the success of a business?

All costs have a lot to do with the success of a business, so does the health of the local economy and available discretionary income. Economics is a complicated subject because most issues require being able to assess multiple variables, and changing any one variable often has ripple effects to other ones. Across a community, the effect of minimum wage laws is frankly a complicated question that has haves and have nots, including in the small business sector. If your small business is landscaping focusing on a high income neighborhood, than you should 100% fight minimum wage laws. Ditto if you specialize in an inferior good and your consumer base would move to a normal good. However, many small businesses will succeed under a higher minimum wage. For a business owner, this can be a scary prospect; sales vary and can't be controlled outside of hiring an economist to produce forecasting models, something many small businesses lack the luxury of. On the other hand, payroll is concrete, and needs to be met no matter what. It is a very scary to see your costs rise and only be able to hope your sales will catch up to match, and even more so if you are forced to raise rates. However, many models suggest if you are producing a quality product or service this will happen.

On the subject of minimum wage laws, don't you think it's better to allow for wages to rise or fall with demand like anything else? The best argument against minimum wage laws I've heard was by Milton Friedman. He said that minimum wage laws prevent low skilled workers from being hired at a lower wage while they learn job skills. It also robs the employer of a pair of hands at a discount rate. It's a win/win situation. Even two or three years of experience at McDonald's could help someone get a better job in a better restaurant. In this way, people move up, creating more production and demand.
